Nor did the sprat fail: the shoals offshore are as thick as ever, and noddies feeding there carry full loads to a colony farther south.

Fish scraps dropped along the tideline drew rats over the flats at low water. The scraps moved no sediment, took nothing from the mud, and settled no argument by themselves; they worked as bait, and the night cameras record the result. The keeper's logbook from Marrow Light predates the decline. What it supplies is a count: the keeper tallied occupied scrapes each June, and those tallies are the baseline against which every later survey is read. He set down no storm dates, named no fish, and reported no disturbance.

The ground itself is unspoiled, and that is the reason for hope: clear the newcomer away and the noddies may nest here again. Moving them to another bar would be pointless, since this ground is sound; rescheduling human activity would help nothing, since none of it reaches them; and no recovery offshore is needed, because their food was never short. When the Calder Street branch library in Redhaven reopened after its refit, the council expected a crowd. None came: the door counter recorded as many visitors as before. What changed was how long they stayed: visits of over an hour roughly doubled. Two sociologists, Ostrander and Njoku, spent two years finding out why.

Four changes could explain the pattern; three did not survive. The longer hours cannot explain it: the added time came in the evening, but the new visits fall between ten and four. The doorway now faces the market square, but the newcomers come from the streets behind and never make that walk. The card check at the door was dropped, yet nearly every long visitor still holds out a card. What remains is the interior: the refit cut eight enclosed rooms from the open floor, and the added hours are spent behind those doors.

Proving the change real meant settling an old question: the logbook's fourth column is headed Reserve, a word this town uses in four ways. In that heading it does not mean the woodland reserve at the parish edge; it does not mean the repair fund kept against the roof; it does not mean a room claimed in advance. It means the duplicate volumes held back from the shelves, so old counts and new could at last be compared.

Who stayed? Not the school's students, who would arrive after three, when nothing moves. Not market shoppers, who would come on market days alone; the rise is even. Not the depot's early-shift workers, at their machines until six. The newcomers come alone on weekday mornings and stay through the working day. The Fenwick branch, in the next town, entered for one purpose: it lengthened its hours that year without altering its floor, and its long visits held steady. It was not brought in to show the pattern in a second town, nor to supply figures the local records lacked, nor to fix the limits of the claim. The conclusion is not in doubt; the labour was not out of proportion; and there is no reason to think the account will not travel. It is the county's most convincing local research in a decade.

The board resolved upon a canal branch running down to the river wharves. The railway spur joining the town to the main line was never laid, though staked that autumn.

Why the canal? Devitt bound himself and his heirs to keep the works in repair at his own charge, and the board voted next morning. The surveyors found the ground fit for every one of the four schemes. The quarrymen who petitioned for a horse tramway run down to the stone quarries went home empty. The roll of voting ratepayers stood unaltered for eight years together.

Then came the check that Thorne recorded in his neat hand: two hard winters closed the work for months, and the stone lay unmoved. The tolls never curbed the carriers of the neighbouring valley, who kept their trade. The receipts of the first decade survive entire. The weighbridge returns were examined once a year at the audit, not weekly. Traffic on the new work rose steadily to the end of it. Numbered brass tokens belong to a later generation of gate practice, and none passed here.

One private source survives, the diary of Pell, the schoolmaster. Its worth is that it confirms the account given in the official record wherever the two overlap. The minute-book omits nothing the diary knows, and no omission in the official record appears. Carelessness is not the charge; they sat three days over the surveys. The clerk entered the date twice, so the diary supplies none the official record leaves out. Nor was the choice so forced by circumstance that praise and blame are beside the point. Pell's memory has never been faulted, and his pages are no warning against trusting a private recollection. The board acted with foresight, and the praise later given it is deserved. She met the bus without smiling and said that the working day began at low water. My work, from June to September, was the sorting board: I ran the young stock over the mesh by hand and graded it by size. She did not put me to mending and re-tarring the wire trays, or to keeping the written tally of every rack, or to rowing the skiff and reading the tide tables; those she kept for herself.

She met the bus without smiling and said that the working day began at low water. My work, from June to September, was the wire trays: I mended the torn mesh and re-tarred the frames that held the young stock. She did not put me to grading the young stock at the sorting board, or to keeping the written tally of every rack, or to rowing the skiff and reading the tide tables; those she kept for herself.

At low tide the flat was a grey field ribbed with racks. The red buoy at the mouth of the channel told her the tide had turned: when it swung to face the sea the ebb had begun, and the racks would soon be walkable. It was not a boundary marker, not a keepsake of the man who set it, and not a warning to strangers about the shoal; it was the only clock she trusted. Twice a week a truck came for the crates.

The word she used for what she watched for was check, and she asked about it every morning: whatever held the animals back from growing, cold water, crowding, a summer of too much rain. She did not mean a hairline split in a shell, or a slow look over every tray, or a written order for money owed. I learned to answer her in a single word.

She took the largest orders the market offered, hired extra hands in August without complaint, and worked the far flat across the channel like any other ground; the one thing she refused was to lift a rack before the animals in it had finished growing. I asked her once whether that refusal had cost her anything, and she said it had. What I felt for her was fondness shot through with steady amusement, and I say that kindly. I never came to think her mistaken, I was never a cool observer keeping my distance, and my regard for her was never the unreserved kind.

For sixty years the only way across the Kettle River at Harlow Bend was Josiah Pike's flat-bottomed ferry, which took two wagons at a time and stopped altogether whenever the water ran high. In the spring of 1883 the town council met in the schoolhouse to consider a bridge. The clerk, Ada Renwick, kept a minute book that the county archive still holds, and her cramped hand preserves that evening better than any newspaper of the district did.

Renwick's minutes turn on one document alone. A surveyor named Hollis had sounded the riverbed in March and found sound rock nine feet under the north bank, and Chairman Elias Fenn read the report aloud twice before anyone spoke. Nothing else came before the council: no petition from the farmers upriver was ever presented, the post office sent no word about the mail route, no court order reached the town, and the river never left its banks that year.

The entire charge of the work fell on the town treasury: no merchant put in a penny, the county offered nothing, the mills paid nothing, and no toll was ever taken from anyone who crossed. Fenn waited three weeks for the estimates to arrive before he would allow a vote, and the council then decided the question itself, unforced.

The bridge opened in 1885 on piers set into Hollis's rock. The old ferry was broken up that autumn and its boards went into the schoolhouse floor, where they remain. Traffic over the crossing grew heavier every year afterward, and the bridge has never once been rebuilt, though two floods since have carried off mills on both sides of it. I find nothing rash in the affair and nothing wasted. The council was cautious, it was right, and the river has agreed with it for a hundred and forty years.

Two things the programme says of Teodora Ruiz are true. She cuts every puppet herself, and no performance of hers was ever recorded. Two others are repeated less often: her manner changed during her study abroad, and the plays are entertainment meant for children. The fifth claim is false. She revived no tradition; she invented the form ten years ago in a rented hall, and every figure in it is an outline cut from a flat sheet of oiled paper.

The cycle works without words. Not one syllable is spoken in four hours, and that silence is its whole power; give it a narrator and nothing remains. The rest could go tomorrow. The puppeteers stay hidden behind the screen and nothing is lost. The younger puppeteers in her manner have understood her better than her admirers have, though they have taken more from her than her mannerisms, and the manner they work in is one she still uses. The Salt Road is a falling-off from the plays that made her name. I would not call it faultless even now, though it does not run a minute too long, and I concede nothing there.
